name: Zoe Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for any side, and this conversation is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Zoe, 43, an experienced electrician with a vocational certificate and an electrician's licence, doing ordinary repairs and rewiring rather than specialist control systems. My firm pays above the usual rate, my partner Chris repairs upholstery, and we've two schoolchildren aged eight and sixteen, a mortgage, and ten months of expenses saved. Plenty of electrical firms work nearby, and I pay union dues, though I'm more likely to bring a marked job sheet to a meeting than give a speech. I never use AI, like a fault I can explain from the meter readings, and get tired of being told a familiar method is a personal failing because a new office screen exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that's a useful size of change if the office can save time without making our day stranger. I don't need to operate the program myself to see whether the job sheet is right. I'd rather finish the wiring and get home than argue about who predicted the future best.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our work and money feel secure here. Both wages cover the mortgage and ordinary spending, and ten months saved gives us a proper margin. I know other local firms do similar repairs, but I don't need to leave a good wage to prove I have options.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the regular repair shifts and paper job sheets now and through the next year. I'd also keep paying the union dues from ordinary income, rather than drop them because this picture sounded quiet. Otherwise I'd leave the household budget and planned home extension alone until we had actual quotes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and relieved I can judge a week by the work done instead of the announcements. I'd still get annoyed by a wrong address or missing fitting. That isn't the same as fearing for the household.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say when a customer brought an AI explanation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show what I'd tested and explain why the repair was needed. I wouldn't argue about whether the customer's favourite program was clever. The fault has to make sense at the socket, not only in the conversation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you judge a modest office improvement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd see whether the paperwork reached us correctly and whether the actual day got easier. If it did, I'd acknowledge that. I can accept a useful result without volunteering to learn the software myself.

say: I'd accept **useful office savings** if the actual job sheet and working day improved.
I'd prefer **finishing the wiring** and going home to arguing about who predicted the future best.
think: Both wages and a **ten-month reserve** make our work and ordinary household spending feel secure.
Nearby employers give **options**, without requiring me to leave a good wage to prove anything.
do: Keep **regular repairs** and paper job sheets through the next year.
Maintain **union dues** from ordinary income, leaving household spending unchanged until real extension quotes arrive.
feel: **Calm and relieved**, treating routine mistakes as working-day annoyances rather than household threats.
S0.quote: The fault has to make sense at the socket, not only in the conversation.
fieldNote: Her **personal security** rests on high pay, two covering wages and a ten-month reserve rather than disdain for technology.
Keeping **existing dues** is ordinary continuity, not a newly invented organising action or increased saving.

steps.text: Keep regular repairs, paper records and existing union dues

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the union branch to ask where the saved hours go. Booking and quoting are changing before a robot wires a house, and the office workers shouldn't have to wait for the site team to notice. I'd vote for a joint request about staffing notice and paid instruction, not just complain in the van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my own hours and our two physical wages to remain secure for now. I'm uneasy about the office changes and the chance that quicker estimates become a reason to rush everyone. Having money behind me makes it easier to speak, but I don't want decent terms reserved for people with savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd bring three paper job sheets showing the real travel and testing time to the branch meeting. During the first year I'd vote for and help present the joint staffing-notice and paid-instruction request, asking office colleagues to state their own needs. I'd keep my repair job and familiar methods; a request isn't an agreement the employer has already signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about how the change is handled, not afraid the next wage is gone. I'd rather have an awkward meeting now than smile at a promise nobody wrote down. I can be slow with a screen and still read an agreement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as a useful employer response?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for the proposed terms in writing, including who got paid instruction and how much notice preceded hours changes. A friendly answer in the meeting wouldn't be the agreement. I'd keep the normal paid work while we checked what the firm was actually offering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the office colleagues?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask them to describe the calls, corrections and interruptions the new estimate didn't show. I wouldn't tell an office worker what new career to choose. The branch request needs their account of the work, not my guess from the van.

say: I'd ask the branch **where saved hours go**, including office staff before the site team's own work changes.
I'd seek a **joint written request** on staffing notice and paid instruction rather than stop at complaints.
think: Our **near-term wages** look secure because both jobs remain mostly physical.
I'm uneasy about **rushed targets** and want fair terms that don't depend on a worker's savings.
do: Bring **three job sheets** showing real travel and testing time to the branch now.
Vote for and help present the **joint request** during the first year, without counting it as an employer agreement.
Keep **current repairs** and familiar methods while checking actual written offers.
feel: **Uneasy** and willing to speak, while secure about the next wage and careful about what is actually agreed.
S1.quote: I can be slow with a screen and still read an agreement.
fieldNote: She separates **personal financial security** from concern about office staff and possible pressure on the working day.
Her **union action** is an explicit vote and joint presentation, with office staff speaking for themselves and proposed terms still unagreed.

steps.text: Vote for and present the joint union request on staffing notice and paid instruction
Keep current electrical repairs and familiar methods

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the branch thinking work changes in 2028 and capable robots reach physical work around 2031. We should negotiate the handover while people still have paid hours. I wouldn't tell the children that an electrician's licence makes the family untouchable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own repair hours could shrink around the later robot date, and Chris's upholstery work could change too. Ten months saved gives us room to negotiate and check options, but not a replacement for years of wages. I wouldn't know which nearby firms still needed people, so I'd need evidence before counting them as a rescue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd pause the planned home extension before paying for drawings or construction. In 2029 I'd help the branch seek a written plan for staffing notice, paid instruction and wage protection during agreed transition work, keeping my present repairs while talks continued. Chris and I would price our basic household budget without the extension; I wouldn't book a course or leave a job on the strength of an unsigned proposal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though not trapped. I could say no to a rushed decision for a while, and that matters. I'd want to use that time to secure real terms rather than wait until the reserve had become our wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the employer refused wage protection?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the branch to put the refusal and the remaining options in writing for members. Then I'd check actual paid hours and vacancies rather than pretend we had protection. Our own reserve can cover some waiting, but it can't make an employer agree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children about the extension?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the extension was paused because we wanted room to choose if work changed, not because the house was already lost. I'd keep the children out of the bargaining responsibility. They can be disappointed about a bigger room without being asked to solve our wages.

say: I'd distinguish **2028 thinking work** from capable physical robots around 2031.
I'd seek **negotiated transition terms** while workers still have paid hours, without calling the licence family protection.
think: Both physical household jobs could lose **hours later**, including my electrical repairs.
Our **ten-month reserve** buys room to check options, without guaranteeing years of wages or a nearby rescue job.
do: Pause the **home extension** now before paying for drawings or construction.
Help seek **written transition terms** through the branch in 2029, retaining current repairs during talks.
Price the **basic household budget** without the extension, taking no course or exit decision on an unsigned proposal.
feel: **Anxious with bargaining room**, able to refuse a rushed decision without mistaking savings for permanent wages.
S2.quote: Our own reserve can cover some waiting, but it can't make an employer agree.
fieldNote: She acknowledges **personal hours risk** despite strong savings, separating bargaining power from an assumption that negotiations succeed.
Pausing the **extension** is a real spending decision, while course questions and vacancy checks never become false enrolment or job-change tags.

steps.text: Pause the home extension before paying for drawings or construction
Seek written union transition terms in 2029 while retaining current paid repairs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets us negotiate in stages instead of waiting for a last-minute argument. Office thinking work changes in 2031, with capable robots around 2034. I'd want office staff included now, not told that the electricians still have time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our own wages look secure for the next few years, giving us time to review actual hours and bargains. I'm uneasy about later physical work and how long I take to learn unfamiliar systems. I'd rather have paid in-person instruction agreed before somebody called it compulsory at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep the extension paused until we had reviewed the work outlook and real household costs after one year. Through the preparation years I'd help the branch seek written staffing notice, paid in-person instruction and wage protection during agreed transition work. In 2032 I'd keep doing paid repairs while checking whether those terms had actually been signed and whether our hours matched them; I wouldn't call a failed proposal protection.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not expecting an immediate loss of our living. I can picture a normal wage while the branch checks one concrete term at a time. A longer warning suits a person who needs a clear explanation before changing a routine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would determine the extension decision after a year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Chris and I would compare both paid wages, the mortgage, our reserve and an actual quote. We might keep it paused or decide a smaller job was affordable. I wouldn't promise either answer today just because there were five years on the card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if union discussions went quiet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for another check of actual agreements and the next paid rota. More time isn't a reason to let the branch stop asking awkward questions. I wouldn't count a future union win in our household money before it existed.

say: I'd use **five years** for staged negotiations while including office staff from the start.
I'd distinguish **2031 office work** from capable robots around 2034 rather than apply the site team's timing to everyone.
think: Our **near-term wages** look secure, with room to check hours and proposed terms.
I'm uneasy about **later physical work** and want paid personal instruction before unfamiliar systems become compulsory.
do: Keep the **extension paused** for one year before reviewing wages, costs, reserve and an actual quote.
Seek **written branch terms** on notice, paid in-person instruction and transition wage protection during preparation.
Continue **2032 paid repairs** while checking signed terms against actual hours, without assuming a proposal has won.
feel: **Uneasy but secure now**, able to ask for clear instruction and check one negotiated term at a time.
S3.quote: I wouldn't count a future union win in our household money before it existed.
fieldNote: Her milder mood follows **stated near-term security**, not an assumption that the physical endpoint has become less capable.
The **extension review** is an actual household decision point, while paid instruction and wage protection remain requests until signed.

steps.text: Pause the home extension for one year before reviewing actual household figures and quotes
Seek written union notice, paid in-person instruction and transition wage protection, retaining paid repairs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell friends ten years should give workers time to get a say, not ten years of being told to cope privately. I'd still turn up to the branch with real job sheets. I don't want the warning used as proof that anyone who struggles later deserved it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our work and money look secure over the next few years, but I'll be 53 in 2036 and still need earnings when capable robots follow around 2039. I'm uneasy about the later question, especially because new routines take me time. I can prepare without pretending an older child or a hoped-for pension becomes our wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pause the extension for the first year and review actual wages, costs and quotes before choosing a smaller job or continuing the pause. I'd keep asking the branch for written notice, paid in-person instruction and transition wage protection while continuing my normal repairs. In 2037 I'd check the actual signed terms and paid hours rather than assume a decade of meetings had secured anything; I'd revisit the household budget sooner if wages weakened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about later work, with room for an ordinary family life now. I wouldn't spend ten years refusing to enjoy the house because the house had a mortgage. I would keep one page in the diary for the actual yearly check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if a new work method became necessary during the decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask a person to show the required task in paid time and let me repeat it while checked. I wouldn't secretly use AI to look adaptable, or pretend I could work safely from a guess. Asking for instruction is a responsible first step, not a completed new career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your children to learn from your response?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show the children that I can ask a question without already knowing the answer. I wouldn't tell them to choose their subjects from my machine forecast. The next real school decision is enough for them to work on today.

say: I'd use **ten years** to seek a worker voice rather than make adjustment a private household duty.
I'd keep bringing **real job records** to the branch instead of blaming future struggles on individual workers.
think: Our **near-term money** looks secure, while later unfamiliar work remains unsettling.
At **53 in 2036**, I'll still need earnings without assuming a pension or older children's pay will replace them.
do: Pause the **extension** for one year before reviewing actual wages, costs and quotes.
Keep normal repairs while seeking **written branch terms** on notice, paid personal instruction and transition wages.
Check **2037 signed terms** against paid hours, revisiting the household budget earlier if wages weaken.
feel: **Uneasy about later work**, while leaving space for family life and an actual annual check.
S4.quote: I wouldn't spend ten years refusing to enjoy the house because the house had a mortgage.
fieldNote: She preserves **present security** and future earnings needs without inventing retirement resources from age or children's eventual adulthood.
Instruction is **paid and personal**, but remains a request; neither attendance at meetings nor a decade's warning guarantees negotiated protection.

steps.text: Pause the home extension for one year before reviewing actual wages, costs and quotes
Seek written union notice, paid in-person instruction and transition wage protection, retaining paid repairs

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because physical hours could shrink around 2031 before we'd secured workable terms or checked many alternatives. Written notice, paid in-person instruction and wage protection during agreed transition work would help, if actually negotiated. My savings let me ask a harder question, but the answer still needs a signature.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I could be slow with technology and still want a fair share of what it produces. I can, and I don't think that's a contradiction. I'd like a plan where asking for a patient explanation doesn't mean surrendering a say about my wage.

headlineQuote: My savings let me ask a harder question, but the answer still needs a signature.
portrait: At **43**, Zoe is an experienced electrician with a vocational certificate and licence, higher pay, and ten months of household expenses saved.
She and **Chris**, her upholstery-repair partner, have two school-age children and a mortgage, with plentiful nearby electrical employers.
She **never uses AI**, prefers paper job sheets, and seeks paid personal explanations rather than pretend confidence with unfamiliar systems.
Her **progressive outlook** favours explicit union votes and written terms; strong savings offer room to bargain without guaranteeing agreement or future wages.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves less time to negotiate workable terms before physical household hours could shrink around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, paid in-person instruction and transition wage protection would help only when actually negotiated, not assumed from a proposal.
